subQuestions.label: 1(a)(1)
subQuestions.questionText:
A jewellery manufacturer measured the diameters of 400 gold spheres produced by machine A and another 400 produced by machine B. The results are shown as cumulative frequency (ogive) curves (diameter in mm on the horizontal axis, cumulative frequency on the vertical axis).

Determine the interquartile range for the diameters of gold spheres produced by machine A.
subQuestions.memoText:
From the machine A ogive: lower quartile $Q_1 = 5{,}8$ mm; upper quartile $Q_3 = 6{,}0$ mm.
$\text{IQR} = 6{,}0 - 5{,}8 = 0{,}2$ mm

subQuestions.label: 1(a)(2)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine the 50th percentile for the diameters of gold spheres produced by machine A.
subQuestions.memoText: $P_{50}$: $50\% \times 400 = 200$th value $\Rightarrow P_{50} = 5{,}9$ mm

subQuestions.label: 1(a)(3)
subQuestions.questionText: If the gold spheres with diameters less than or equal to 5,9 mm are considered defective, determine the percentage of defective gold spheres produced by machine B.
subQuestions.memoText:
From the machine B ogive, $100$ spheres have diameter $\leq 5{,}9$ mm.
$\dfrac{100}{400} \times 100\% = 25\%$ defective

subQuestions.label: 1(b)(1)
subQuestions.questionText:
In a school, learners were surveyed about the time they spent on the internet over a weekend. The results are shown as a box-and-whisker plot (minimum $\approx 1$, $Q_1 = 2$, median $= 5$, $Q_3 = 6$, maximum $= 7$ hours).

Is the data positively or negatively skewed?
subQuestions.memoText: Negatively skewed.

subQuestions.label: 1(b)(2)
subQuestions.questionText:
Consider the statement: 'The percentage of learners that spent from 2 to 5 hours on the internet is almost three times as much as the percentage of learners that spent from 6 to 7 hours on the internet.'

Is the statement true or false?
subQuestions.memoText: False. $25\%$ of the data lies between $Q_1$ and the median (2 to 5 hours) and $25\%$ lies between $Q_3$ and the maximum (6 to 7 hours) — the percentages are equal, not a factor of three apart.

subQuestions.label: 1(b)(3)
subQuestions.questionText: One of the learners was not included in the data represented in the box-and-whisker plot above. If the learner spent 10 hours on the internet over the weekend, determine whether the learner is an outlier or not. Use the formula $Q_3 + 1{,}5 \times \text{IQR}$.
subQuestions.memoText:
From the box plot: $Q_1 = 2$, $Q_3 = 6$, so $\text{IQR} = 4$.
$Q_3 + 1{,}5 \times \text{IQR} = 6 + 1{,}5 \times 4 = 12$
Since $10 < 12$, the learner is not an outlier.

questions.title: Analytical Geometry — Parallel & Perpendicular Lines; Isosceles Triangle

subQuestions.label: 2(a)
subQuestions.questionText:
In the diagram, $A(-3; 10)$ and B (in the first quadrant) are points on quadrilateral ABCD. The equation of line DC is $y = -\dfrac{1}{3}x - 1$, and DC forms an angle $\theta$ with the $x$-axis as indicated.

Determine the size of $\theta$.
subQuestions.memoText:
$\tan\theta = \left|-\dfrac{1}{3}\right|$
$\theta = 18{,}4°$

subQuestions.label: 2(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine the equation of the line AB if AB // DC.

subQuestions.label: 2(c)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine the equation of the line AD if AD $\perp$ DC.
subQuestions.memoText:
$m_{AD} = 3$ (perpendicular to DC).
$y = 3x + c$; using $A(-3; 10)$: $10 = 3(-3) + c \Rightarrow c = 19$
$y = 3x + 19$

subQuestions.label: 2(d)(1)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine the coordinates of D and hence calculate the length of AD.
subQuestions.memoText:
D is the intersection of $y = 3x + 19$ and $y = -\dfrac{1}{3}x - 1$:
$3x + 19 = -\dfrac{1}{3}x - 1 \Rightarrow \dfrac{10}{3}x = -20 \Rightarrow x = -6$; $y = 3(-6) + 19 = 1$, so $D(-6; 1)$.
$AD = \sqrt{(-3 - (-6))^2 + (10 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 81} = \sqrt{90} = 3\sqrt{10} \approx 9{,}5$ units.

subQuestions.label: 2(d)(2)
subQuestions.questionText: If it is further given that the equation of the line BC is $x = 6$, show that $\triangle$ABD is isosceles.
subQuestions.memoText:
B is on AB with $x = 6$: $y = -\dfrac{1}{3}(6) + 9 = 7$, so $B(6; 7)$.
$AB = \sqrt{(6 - (-3))^2 + (7 - 10)^2} = \sqrt{81 + 9} = \sqrt{90} = 3\sqrt{10}$.
$AD = 3\sqrt{10}$ (from (d)(1)).
Since $AB = AD$, $\triangle$ABD is isosceles.

subQuestions.label: 3(a)(1)
subQuestions.questionText:
The test scores of 5 students are given in ascending order as $\{25; x + 3; x + 6; x + 9; x + 13\}$. The median is 41.

Determine the value of $x$.
subQuestions.memoText: The median is the 3rd value: $x + 6 = 41 \Rightarrow x = 35$

subQuestions.label: 3(a)(2)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine the standard deviation of the scores using your answer to (a)(1).
subQuestions.memoText:
Scores: $\{25; 38; 41; 44; 48\}$.
Using a calculator: SD $= 7{,}8$

subQuestions.label: 3(a)(3)
subQuestions.questionText: How many scores will lie within one standard deviation from the mean? Show your working.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mean $= 39{,}2$.
One SD from the mean: $39{,}2 - 7{,}8 \leq x \leq 39{,}2 + 7{,}8$, i.e. $31{,}4 \leq x \leq 47$.
Scores in this range: $38$, $41$, $44$ $\Rightarrow$ 3 scores.

subQuestions.label: 3(b)(1)
subQuestions.questionText:
The minimum overnight temperatures ($T$ °C) and the number of service calls ($S$) to a company that supplies gas heaters were recorded over 8 days. The least squares regression line is $S = -1{,}8T + 22{,}7$.

State whether the data represents a positive or negative correlation.
subQuestions.memoText: Negative.

subQuestions.label: 3(b)(2)
subQuestions.questionText: Use the regression line to predict the number of service calls made for an overnight temperature of 10 °C.

subQuestions.label: 3(b)(3)
subQuestions.questionText: The correlation coefficient for the 8-day period is $-0{,}95$. On the 9th day, the number of service calls was 8 and the minimum overnight temperature was 3 °C. If the 9th day data is included, what effect will it have on the correlation coefficient? Explain.
subQuestions.memoText: The regression line predicts $S = -1{,}8(3) + 22{,}7 = 17{,}3$ calls, but the actual value is $8$ — this point lies far from the line. The correlation will still be negative but weaker (less negative).

subQuestions.label: 4(a)
subQuestions.questionText:
Given $f(x) = \sin 3x$ and $g(x) = \cos(x - 30°)$ for $x \in [0°; 180°]$.

Determine the period of the graph of $f$.

subQuestions.label: 4(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine the range of the graph of $g$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Over $x \in [0°; 180°]$, $\cos(x - 30°)$ reaches its maximum $1$ (at $x = 30°$) and its minimum $\cos(180° - 30°) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ (at $x = 180°$).
Range $= \left[-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}; 1\right]$

subQuestions.label: 4(c)
subQuestions.questionText: Show on your graph (using capital letters), for $x \in [0°; 180°]$, the solution(s) to $\sin 3x = \cos(x - 30°)$.
subQuestions.memoText: $\sin 3x = \cos(x - 30°)$ at Points A and B — the points where the graphs of $f$ and $g$ intersect.

subQuestions.label: 4(d)
subQuestions.questionText: Use your graph to determine the solution(s) to $\cos(x - 30°) \geq \sin 3x$ for $x \in [0°; 180°]$.
subQuestions.memoText: $0° \leq x \leq 120°$

subQuestions.label: 5(a)
subQuestions.questionText:
A, D, B and C lie on the circle with centre O, and DB = BC.

If $\hat{A} = x$, state, with reasons, two other angles equal to $x$.
subQuestions.memoText:
$\hat{C}_2 = x$ (angles in the same segment — subtended by chord DB).
$\hat{D}_3 = x$ (isosceles $\triangle$BDC — DB = BC, angles opposite equal sides).

subQuestions.label: 5(b)(1)
subQuestions.questionText: Given $\hat{O}_1 = 94°$, determine $\hat{D}_2$.
subQuestions.memoText:
In $\triangle$OCD: $\hat{C}_1 + \hat{D}_2 = 180° - 94°$ (interior angles of $\triangle$).
$\hat{C}_1 = \hat{D}_2$ (CO and OD are radii; angles opposite equal sides).
$\therefore \hat{D}_2 = \dfrac{180° - 94°}{2} = 43°$

subQuestions.label: 5(b)(2)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine $\hat{B}_1 + \hat{B}_2$.
subQuestions.memoText:
$\hat{O}_2 = 360° - 94° = 266°$ (angles around a point).
$\hat{B}_1 + \hat{B}_2 = \dfrac{266°}{2} = 133°$ (angle at centre $= 2 \times$ angle at circle).

subQuestions.label: 5(b)(3)
subQuestions.questionText: Hence or otherwise determine $x$.
subQuestions.memoText:
$2x + 133° = 180°$ (interior angles of $\triangle$)
$x = 23\tfrac{1}{2}°$

questions.title: Circle Geometry — Semicircle, Cyclic Quadrilateral & Chord

subQuestions.label: 6(a)
subQuestions.questionText:
A, B, C, D and E lie on the circle with centre O. AC is perpendicular to OB and they intersect at F. AOE is a straight line. $\hat{A}_1 = 38°$.

Determine $\hat{C}_1$.
subQuestions.memoText: $\hat{C}_1 = 90°$ (angle in a semicircle — AOE is a diameter).

subQuestions.label: 6(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine $\hat{D}$.
subQuestions.memoText: $\hat{D} = 180° - 38° = 142°$ (opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral ABCD).

subQuestions.label: 6(c)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine $A\hat{B}C$.
subQuestions.memoText:
$\hat{E}_1 = 180° - (38° + 90°) = 52°$ (interior angles of $\triangle$ACE).
$\hat{B} = 180° - 52° = 128°$ (opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral).

subQuestions.label: 6(d)
subQuestions.questionText: If AC = 8 cm and BC = 5 cm, determine the length of BF.
subQuestions.memoText:
$AF = FC$ (line from centre perpendicular to a chord bisects it), so $AF = FC = 4$.
$BC = 5$ (given).
$BF^2 = BC^2 - FC^2 = 25 - 16 = 9$ (Pythagoras)
$\therefore BF = 3$ units

questions.title: Area Rule Proof & Surface Area of a Prism

subQuestions.label: 7(a)
subQuestions.questionText: Prove the area rule stating that Area $\triangle PQR = \dfrac{1}{2}pq\sin\hat{R}$ for any acute-angled triangle $\triangle PQR$.
subQuestions.memoText:
Draw the perpendicular (altitude) from P to QR; let its length be $h$.
In the right-angled triangle formed, $\sin\hat{R} = \dfrac{h}{PR} = \dfrac{h}{q}$, so $h = q\sin\hat{R}$.
Area $\triangle PQR = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times p \times h = \dfrac{1}{2}q(p\sin\hat{R}) = \dfrac{1}{2}pq\sin\hat{R}$.

subQuestions.label: 7(b)
subQuestions.questionText:
A solid right triangular prism has equilateral triangular ends with sides 8 cm and a height (length) of 15 cm.

Calculate the total surface area of the prism.
subQuestions.memoText:
Area of one triangular end $= \dfrac{1}{2}(8)(8)\sin 60° = 16\sqrt{3}$ cm$^2$ (equilateral $\triangle$).
Total surface area $= 3 \times (15 \times 8) + 2 \times (16\sqrt{3}) = 360 + 32\sqrt{3} \approx 415{,}4$ cm$^2$

subQuestions.label: 8(a)
subQuestions.questionText:
Solve for $x$, correct to one decimal place, in the given interval:

$$1 - 2\sin^2 x = -\dfrac{1}{7} \quad \text{for } x \in [-180°; 90°]$$

subQuestions.label: 8(b)
subQuestions.questionText:
Simplify the following to its simplest form:

$$-\cos(\theta) \cdot \cos^3(90° + \theta) - \tan(180° - \theta) \cdot \cos(\theta) \cdot \cos^3(-\theta)$$
subQuestions.memoText:
$\cos(90° + \theta) = -\sin\theta$, so $\cos^3(90° + \theta) = -\sin^3\theta$; $\tan(180° - \theta) = -\tan\theta$; $\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta$.
$= -\cos\theta(-\sin^3\theta) - (-\tan\theta)(\cos\theta)(\cos^3\theta)$
$= \cos\theta\sin^3\theta + \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\cos^4\theta$
$= \cos\theta\sin^3\theta + \sin\theta\cos^3\theta$
$= \sin\theta\cos\theta(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta)$
$= \sin\theta\cos\theta$

questions.title: Analytical Geometry — Circle, Chords & Touching Circles

subQuestions.label: 9(a)
subQuestions.questionText:
A, B, D and the origin O lie on the circle with centre C. The equation of the circle is $x^2 + y^2 + 6x - 8y = 0$, and the equation of line AB is $x - 2y + 21 = 0$.

Determine the centre and the radius of the circle.

subQuestions.label: 9(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine the co-ordinates of A and B.
subQuestions.memoText:
Substitute $x = 2y - 21$ into the circle equation:
$(2y - 21)^2 + y^2 + 6(2y - 21) - 8y = 0$
$4y^2 - 84y + 441 + y^2 + 12y - 126 - 8y = 0$
$5y^2 - 80y + 315 = 0 \Rightarrow y^2 - 16y + 63 = 0 \Rightarrow (y - 7)(y - 9) = 0$
$y = 7$ or $y = 9$, giving $B(-7; 7)$ and $A(-3; 9)$.

subQuestions.label: 9(c)(1)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine the midpoint of AD.
subQuestions.memoText:
D is on the circle with $y = 0$: $x^2 + 6x = 0 \Rightarrow x(x + 6) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0$ or $x = -6$, so $D(-6; 0)$.
Midpoint of AD $= \left(\dfrac{-3 - 6}{2}; \dfrac{9 + 0}{2}\right) = \left(-\dfrac{9}{2}; \dfrac{9}{2}\right)$.

subQuestions.label: 9(c)(2)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine whether CB passes through the midpoint of line AD.
subQuestions.memoText:
$m_{CB} = \dfrac{4 - 7}{-3 - (-7)} = -\dfrac{3}{4}$.
$m_{C,\text{midpt}} = \dfrac{\frac{9}{2} - 4}{-\frac{9}{2} - (-3)} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{-\frac{3}{2}} = -\dfrac{1}{3}$.
Since $m_{CB} \neq m_{C,\text{midpt}}$, the points are not collinear, so CB does not pass through the midpoint of AD.

subQuestions.label: 9(d)
subQuestions.questionText: A second circle with equation $(x - 3)^2 + (y + 4)^2 = 25$ is drawn on the same set of axes. A student claims that the two circles touch each other in one point. Is the student correct? Show all working.
subQuestions.memoText:
Circle 1: centre $(-3; 4)$, $r = 5$. Circle 2: centre $(3; -4)$, $r = 5$.
Distance between centres $= \sqrt{(3 - (-3))^2 + (-4 - 4)^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = 10$.
Sum of radii $= 5 + 5 = 10$.
Since the distance between the centres equals the sum of the radii, the circles touch at one point. The student is correct.

subQuestions.questionText:
ABCD represents a closed door 1,2 metres wide and 2,2 metres in length. When the door is opened $42°$ along its hinge AD, its new position is represented by AEFD.

Determine the size of $F\hat{A}C$.
subQuestions.memoText:
In $\triangle DCF$: $DC = DF = 1{,}2$ m (door width).
Cosine rule: $CF^2 = (1{,}2)^2 + (1{,}2)^2 - 2(1{,}2)(1{,}2)\cos 42° = 0{,}7397 \Rightarrow CF = 0{,}86$ m.
In $\triangle ADF$: $AF^2 = (2{,}2)^2 + (1{,}2)^2$ (Pythagoras) $\Rightarrow AF = 2{,}506$; and $AF = AC$ (both diagonals of the door).
In $\triangle ACF$: $\cos F\hat{A}C = \dfrac{(2{,}506)^2 + (2{,}506)^2 - (0{,}86)^2}{2(2{,}506)(2{,}506)} = 0{,}9411$
$F\hat{A}C \approx 19{,}8°$

subQuestions.label: 11(a)
subQuestions.questionText:
Prove the following identity:

$$\dfrac{1 + \sin 2x + \sin^2 x - \cos^2 x}{1 + 2\sin x\cos x + \cos 2x} = \tan x$$
subQuestions.memoText:
Numerator: $1 + 2\sin x\cos x + \sin^2 x - \cos^2 x = (\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x) + 2\sin x\cos x + \sin^2 x - \cos^2 x = 2\sin^2 x + 2\sin x\cos x = 2\sin x(\sin x + \cos x)$.
Denominator: $1 + 2\sin x\cos x + (\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x) = (\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x) + 2\sin x\cos x + \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = 2\cos^2 x + 2\sin x\cos x = 2\cos x(\cos x + \sin x)$.
LHS $= \dfrac{2\sin x(\sin x + \cos x)}{2\cos x(\cos x + \sin x)} = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \tan x = $ RHS.

subQuestions.label: 11(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine the values of $x$ for which the identity given in (a) is not valid.
subQuestions.memoText:
The identity is undefined where the denominator $2\cos x(\cos x + \sin x) = 0$:
- $\cos x = 0$ (and $\tan x$ undefined): $x = 90° + k\cdot 180°$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.
- $\cos x + \sin x = 0 \Rightarrow \tan x = -1 \Rightarrow x = -45° + k\cdot 180°$ (i.e. $x = 135° + k\cdot 180°$), $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.

subQuestions.label: 12(a)
subQuestions.questionText:
$\triangle$ABC is given with E and G on AB and D on AC, with AG = GB and ED // GC. F is on CG and D on AC with DF // AB.

Prove: $\dfrac{CF}{FG} = \dfrac{GE}{EA}$.
subQuestions.memoText:
$\dfrac{CF}{FG} = \dfrac{CD}{DA}$ (line DF // AG — line parallel to one side of $\triangle$CGA).
$\dfrac{CD}{DA} = \dfrac{GE}{EA}$ (line ED // GC — line parallel to one side of $\triangle$AGC).
$\therefore \dfrac{CF}{FG} = \dfrac{GE}{EA}$

subQuestions.label: 12(b)
subQuestions.questionText: If $\dfrac{CF}{FG} = \dfrac{2}{1}$, determine the ratio of GE : GA.
subQuestions.memoText:
$\dfrac{GE}{EA} = \dfrac{2}{1}$ (from (a)). With $EA = \dfrac{1}{3}GA$:
$\dfrac{EG}{\frac{1}{3}GA} = \dfrac{2}{1} \Rightarrow GE = \dfrac{2}{3}GA$
$\therefore GE : GA = 2 : 3$

subQuestions.label: 12(c)
subQuestions.questionText: Determine the numerical value of DF : AB.
subQuestions.memoText:
$GE = \dfrac{2}{3}GA$ (proven).
G is the midpoint of AB, so $GA = \dfrac{1}{2}AB$: $GE = \dfrac{2}{3}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}AB\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}AB$.
$DF = EG$ (opposite sides of the parallelogram DEGF), so $DF = \dfrac{1}{3}AB$.
$\therefore DF : AB = 1 : 3$

subQuestions.label: 13(a)
subQuestions.questionText:
The circumscribed circle for $\triangle$BCF is given. AB and AC are tangents to the circle at B and C respectively. FE, FG and FD are perpendiculars from F to AB, F to BC and F to AC.

Prove: $\triangle$FEB is similar to $\triangle$FGC.
subQuestions.memoText:
In $\triangle$FEB and $\triangle$FGC:
$\hat{E}_2 = \hat{G}_1$ (both $= 90°$, given — FE $\perp$ AB, FG $\perp$ BC).
$\hat{B}_1 = \hat{C}_2$ (tan-chord theorem).
$\therefore \triangle$FEB $\;|||\;$ $\triangle$FGC ($\angle$; $\angle$; $\angle$).

subQuestions.label: 13(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Prove: $FG^2 = FE \times FD$.
subQuestions.memoText:
In $\triangle$FDC and $\triangle$FGB:
$\hat{D}_2 = \hat{G}_2$ (both $= 90°$, given).
$\hat{C}_1 = \hat{B}_2$ (tan-chord theorem).
$\therefore \triangle$FDC $\;|||\;$ $\triangle$FGB, so $\dfrac{FD}{FG} = \dfrac{DC}{GB} = \dfrac{FC}{FB}$ (similar triangles, sides in proportion).
From (a): $\dfrac{FE}{FG} = \dfrac{EB}{GC} = \dfrac{FB}{FC}$.
So $\dfrac{FD}{FG} = \dfrac{FC}{FB}$ and $\dfrac{FG}{FE} = \dfrac{FC}{FB}$, giving $\dfrac{FD}{FG} = \dfrac{FG}{FE}$.
$\therefore FG^2 = FE \times FD$.

subQuestions.label: 14(a)
subQuestions.questionText: If $2\cos 2\alpha + \sin 2\alpha = R\cos(2\alpha - \beta)$ where $R > 0$ and $\beta$ is an acute angle, determine $R$ and $\beta$.
subQuestions.memoText:
RHS $= R(\cos 2\alpha\cos\beta + \sin 2\alpha\sin\beta) = R\cos\beta\cos 2\alpha + R\sin\beta\sin 2\alpha$.
Comparing coefficients: $R\cos\beta = 2$ and $R\sin\beta = 1$.
Square and add: $R^2(\cos^2\beta + \sin^2\beta) = 4 + 1 = 5 \Rightarrow R^2 = 5 \Rightarrow R = \sqrt{5}$ (since $R > 0$).
$\sin\beta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \Rightarrow \beta = 26{,}6°$.

subQuestions.label: 14(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Hence, or otherwise, determine the maximum value of $4\cos^2\alpha + \sin 2\alpha$.
subQuestions.memoText:
$4\cos^2\alpha + \sin 2\alpha = 2(\cos 2\alpha + 1) + \sin 2\alpha = 2\cos 2\alpha + \sin 2\alpha + 2 = \sqrt{5}\cos(2\alpha - \beta) + 2$.
The maximum of $\sqrt{5}\cos(2\alpha - \beta)$ is $\sqrt{5}$, so the maximum value is $\sqrt{5} + 2$.
